name: Rafael Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government; we don't sell anything or campaign. What you say is confidential, so you can separate your public answer from your private one. What does a regular day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and I run the supplier payments team at a large packaging company's branch office. I check the disputed bills, approve the monthly payment run and take the calls when a supplier says we shorted them. Eight people bring me the awkward cases; I usually know which delivery note to ask for before they finish the story.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that suits you, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that a supplier can ring at nine angry and be paid correctly by lunch. I did an MBA, but I'm paid less than managers at the main office because this town has its own pay band. Rent and my student loan leave less than a month's expenses in savings, and there aren't many other management offices here. The worst bit is head office calling a late payment a 'process issue' when I have to tell a real person to wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype sounds like the payment software we already have: useful when invoices match, a nuisance when they don't. Head office is also asking us to clear a backlog without overtime. So I wouldn't call my own position comfortable just because AI levels off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the eight people on my team that a machine can match invoice numbers, but we'll still settle the exceptions. I'd ask them to keep the paper trail clean. I wouldn't make a speech about technology to friends; I'm more concerned with next month's rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relieved, but I still worry our branch will lose a post when someone retires. I'm good at this work, yet the local pay band doesn't leave room to save. I'd rather keep a known problem than gamble on a tool I haven't tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll clear the oldest disputed supplier bills with my team every Friday and document why we changed each one. Through the first year of a plateau I'd stay in this role, send an internal pay review request in January and use any raise to build a one-month cash buffer. If the raise is refused, I'd still stay while I look at the few local openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a small relief, not a holiday. The rent and loan are still due even if AI stays dull.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound relieved, but you also say you're short of cash. What happens on a bad month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car needed a new clutch in September and I put it on a card. Another repair would mean asking my sister to cover part of the rent, which I don't want. That's why I need the buffer even in the easy picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the pay request say, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the figures: disputes closed, late-payment fees avoided and the eight people I supervise. I don't expect head office to be sentimental. I'd ask for the main-office team lead rate and settle for a smaller rise if it gets the card paid down.

say: Our **payment exceptions** still need a person to check the delivery notes.
I'll ask the team to keep a **clean paper trail** for every supplier dispute.
think: I'm **relieved** that the payment role would largely remain.
The **local pay band** and thin savings still make a bad month hard to absorb.
do: Clear the **oldest disputes** with my team each Friday.
Request the **main-office pay rate** in January using fee and backlog figures.
Use any rise to build a **one-month buffer** and pay the card down.
feel: I feel **relief**, with the usual rent and loan worry underneath.
S0.quote: The rent and loan are still due even if AI stays dull.
fieldNote: His **current money strain** makes the low-change picture anxious, despite strong standing at work.
He trusts **delivery notes** and named decisions, and treats routine matching differently from settling supplier disputes.
He would seek **better pay internally** before trying a scarce local opening.

steps.text: Clear the oldest supplier disputes with the team every Friday
Put any January pay rise toward a one-month cash buffer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing replies, checking bills and planning payment runs are most of my desk. If software takes those, head office could keep one person to handle the arguments and cut the rest. The warehouses still need hands for a while, but my office doesn't move boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we should test every automatic payment against the delivery notes before anyone signs off. To friends I'd say there may be fewer office jobs here, even if new work appears somewhere else. I wouldn't post a cheerful promise I couldn't back up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think they'd call the cuts 'natural turnover' and leave me to explain them. My record might keep me employed, but my pay could be frozen while the team shrinks. I have no spare money to leave first or retrain without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask finance for a written count of which payment tasks they plan to automate, then have my team log each wrong match for six weeks. If a pilot starts next year, I'd volunteer to sign off only the disputed bills and ask for that duty in my job description. I'd stop eating out on Fridays and put the saved money toward the card balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tight in the chest picturing empty desks near mine. I could still steer the work a bit, but I can't promise my people jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person on the team comes to mind when you say empty desks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mira has handled supplier calls for twelve years and knows when a missing note means a truck never arrived. Head office sees her as someone who types replies. I'd tell her what the pilot covers as soon as I have it in writing, though I can't say she should feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have never used an AI tool. Would you try the pilot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch it first on old bills, with Mira beside me, and compare each answer to our records. If it made fewer mistakes, I'd use it for matching, but I wouldn't let it approve a dispute unseen. My resistance is to trusting a black box with a supplier's money, not to pressing a button.

say: We need **delivery-note checks** before automatic payments go out.
New work may appear, but **fewer local office desks** could remain.
think: Head office may call cuts **natural turnover** and leave me to tell the team.
My **job might survive**, though a frozen wage and smaller team would hurt.
do: Ask finance for the **automation plan** in writing this month.
Log **wrong invoice matches** for six weeks before approving a pilot.
Cut **Friday meals out** and pay down my card balance.
feel: I feel **anxious** for my own pay and the people beside me.
S1.quote: My resistance is to trusting a black box with a supplier's money, not to pressing a button.
fieldNote: His **high skill** may protect his role, but he expects a wage freeze and fewer team members.
He asks for **written task lists** and old-bill trials, rather than banning software outright.
Mira's **supplier knowledge** illustrates the judgment a task count could miss.

steps.text: Ask finance for a written list of payment tasks planned for automation
Stop buying Friday meals out and pay the card balance
Compare the pilot with old disputed bills before signing off any payment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Almost any thinking work by 2028 means the exception calls too, not just invoice matching. I can't claim my MBA or my memory for suppliers will beat a cheaper system at that point. The robots in 2031 might leave physical stock checks for people, but a warehouse supervisor's schedules and reports could be automated in 2028 just like my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team the date as stated and ask head office for a written staffing plan, with no talk of certain safety. To friends I'd admit I need to look for a job outside payments. I wouldn't tell a supplier the change was harmless when I couldn't know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my post could disappear in 2028, and I'm scared of being sent home with the card debt and student loan. There are few management jobs in this town, so a new title on my CV won't solve it. My sister could lend me rent once; she can't replace my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before spring 2027 I'd pay the card first by cancelling the gym and taking the bus twice a week, and I'd ask human resources which paid vacancies exist in our local warehouse operation. I'd apply for the open shift supervisor role if its pay and hours cover rent and it includes floor checks of damaged pallets and missing stock, even if it means nights. If AGI lands in 2028 before I move, I'd take the notice period, apply for that actual vacancy and ask my sister for one month's rent only if the wages stop; I know its planning work could be cut before robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm alarmed, plainly. A two-year clock gives me almost no room for a wrong turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take nights, but you dislike risk. How would you decide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for the rota and the exact wage before I sign anything. A course certificate without a funded vacancy won't pay my rent. If the night job is genuinely open and the money works, familiarity stops being the main issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell your sister before borrowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the amount and repayment date, not just that I need help. She has her own bills and shouldn't carry a promise I can't make good. If there is no job offer, I'd ask for a month and keep applying outside town too.

say: I would ask for a **written staffing plan** without promising anyone a safe desk.
I'd tell friends I may need **warehouse supervision**, where hands-on work lasts longer.
think: My **payment role could end** in 2028, before I can build savings.
My sister can help with **one rent payment**, not replace a salary.
do: Cancel the **gym** and pay off the card before spring 2027.
Check the **shift supervisor vacancy** and apply only if pay covers rent.
Ask my sister for **one month's rent** if my wages stop after 2028.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short clock and the lack of cash for a mistake.
S2.quote: A course certificate without a funded vacancy won't pay my rent.
fieldNote: He names **2028** as the desk risk and 2031 as the warehouse robot date.
The **thin cushion** turns a job search into a question of next month's rent.
He would accept unfamiliar night work only with **confirmed pay** and an open post.

steps.text: Cancel the gym and use the fee to clear card debt
Apply for the local warehouse shift supervisor vacancy if its pay covers rent
Ask his sister for one month of rent if wages stop in 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to clear debt, but it doesn't make the payments desk durable after 2031. A warehouse shift supervisor still checks damaged pallets and counts missing stock on the floor, which robots may not do until around 2034. A warehouse job might buy time on floor checks, but its planning work could go in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that we have years to check what posts actually open inside the company. I'd say to friends that a longer warning means you can save and move with care. I wouldn't pretend every office worker here can simply become a warehouse manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish the student loan by 2030 if I keep my present pay and don't take another loan. I might have a small reserve by the time the desk changes, which would let me turn down a bad shift offer. I don't know if the company would keep a human supervisor for the floor checks after moving its planning to AGI, and robots could take even that physical part around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting in January I'd set a standing payment of 180 extra a month on the student loan, using overtime only when it's offered. I'd ask the warehouse manager to let me shadow a shift once a month and check the next real supervisor opening. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd take the paid internal move if there is one; otherwise I'd use my reserve to search nearby towns while I still have severance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but I can breathe with five years. Having money set aside would make the choice mine for once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does the extra 180 come from without a raise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some months it won't, and I'd rather say that than write a perfect plan. I'd stop replacing things that still work and take the two overtime Saturdays the firm offered last quarter. If those Saturdays disappear, the loan finishes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move out of town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a signed offer that pays enough after travel or a higher rent. My sister lives here and I don't want to leave her for a rumour. I'd check three nearby towns first, not pack a box in 2026.

say: We have **five years** to watch for real internal openings.
A longer warning lets people **save and choose**, though office workers cannot all switch roles.
think: I might clear my **student loan by 2030** if overtime and wages hold.
A warehouse role **might buy time** on floor checks, but planning could go in 2031.
do: Pay an extra **180 monthly** toward the student loan when overtime allows.
Shadow **one warehouse shift** each month and check supervisor vacancies.
Search **three nearby towns** after 2031 if no paid internal move opens.
feel: I feel **worried**, but breathing room and savings would give me a choice.
S3.quote: A warehouse job might buy time on floor checks, but its planning work could go in 2031.
fieldNote: He separates **2031 planning exposure** from physical floor checks that robots may take around 2034.
His **180 loan payment** depends on actual overtime, which he openly admits may vanish.
He would move only for a **signed offer** that covers higher rent or travel.

steps.text: Pay up to 180 extra monthly on the student loan when overtime allows
Shadow a warehouse shift monthly and check funded supervisor vacancies
Move to a nearby town after 2031 only for a signed affordable offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 37, and ten years is long enough to learn another line of work without jumping tomorrow. The payment office still faces the thinking system in 2036; warehouse hands-on work gets until about 2039. I don't want to spend ten years assuming my current chair is permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd ask for a schedule of real training and openings, with names attached. I'd tell friends that a decade is useful only if wages keep coming while you prepare. Online I'd probably say nothing; that's never been how I solve a bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could build a real reserve and change to an operations role before 2036, but only if someone will hire me into one. The slow date is kinder, yet the loan and low pay still make every year count. I wouldn't buy expensive training just because a brochure promises a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the warehouse director for a six-month paid rotation, two days a month on the floor and the rest at my desk, if staffing allows. If approved, I'd complete those floor days on paid time, learning stock checks and the shift handover without giving up my current wage. I'd keep paying down the loan and build three months of expenses before spending on a qualification. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd apply to a named operations opening if one exists; if not, I'd stay through notice and search with that reserve while robots are still about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's uneasy rather than frightening. The long runway helps, but the pay band doesn't suddenly become generous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the director refuses the paid rotation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask for one shadow day a quarter and keep my job. I won't resign to prove I'm flexible. I've seen people return from a course to find the promised vacancy was never budgeted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as enough proof to spend on training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written offer or the director's budgeted role list, plus a course the company pays for. If the firm wants me to supervise warehouse work, it can give me time there on the clock. My own savings are for rent when the work stops.

say: Ask for **named openings** and paid training before promising people a new career.
A decade helps only while **wages continue** through preparation.
think: I could build a **three-month reserve** and change roles before 2036.
The **low pay band** still makes expensive unfunded training a bad bet.
do: Complete the **six-month paid rotation** if the director approves it in 2027.
Build **three months of expenses** before paying for any course.
Apply for a **named operations opening** after 2036 if one exists.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with useful time but no guaranteed post or better pay.
S4.quote: My own savings are for rent when the work stops.
fieldNote: He uses the **ten-year window** for a cautious internal move, with no speculative course fees.
A **paid rotation** depends on staffing; he would accept occasional shadowing if refused.
His mood remains **uneasy** because the current wage and job options still constrain him.

steps.text: Complete a six-month paid warehouse rotation if staffing permits in 2027
Build three months of expenses before paying for any course
Apply for a named operations vacancy after 2036 if one opens

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years is barely time to finish paying down my loan, and the payment decisions I make could be handed to software before I have any cash behind me. I'd need a real notice period, paid training I can actually use, and time to apply for a vacancy before my wages stop.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs when an automatic payment is wrong. The supplier calls my desk now, not a machine, and that responsibility doesn't disappear just because the software can choose faster. I might sound old-fashioned, but I'd like a name on the letter.

headlineQuote: The supplier calls my desk now, not a machine, and that responsibility doesn't disappear just because the software can choose faster.
portrait: Rafael is a **27-year-old team lead** who settles supplier payment disputes at a large packaging company.
His **MBA** and strong record have brought responsibility, but his local pay band leaves less than a month saved.
He has **few nearby alternatives** and has never used AI tools, so even routine automation lands amid money worries.
He seeks **written proof** and named responsibility before changing payments; the 2028 deadline leaves him alarmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his payment role before he clears his loan or builds savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **real notice period** and a chance to apply for an actual vacancy before his pay ends.
**Paid training** tied to a job he can use, rather than a vague course.
